Floß.et: From Middle High German vlōz n, m, from Old High German flōz n, ultimately from the root of fließen (“to flow”). Compare Dutch vlot (“raft”), a related but different formation.

Floh.et:
From Middle High German vlō(ch), from Old High German flōh, from Proto-West Germanic *flauh.
Cognate with Dutch vlo, English flea, Icelandic fló.

Flocke.et: From Old High German floccho. Cognate with English flake.

Flotte.et: Borrowed from Middle Low German vlōte, which pertains to fließen (“to flow”). The contemporary form is modelled on French flotte.

Florett.et: Borrowed from French fleuret, from Italian fioretto (“little flower”).

Florian.et: Borrowed from Latin Flōriānus, derivative of Flōrus; name of a 4th century saint, patron of Austria.
